heading: 2 Basic Introduction — 2.1 Introduction, background, problem restatement, 2.3 Problem Analysis
note: Coded range starts at block 22. Blocks 1-9 (control-number header, summary sheet, five summary paragraphs, keywords) and 10-16 (table of contents) are front matter; blocks 17-21 are a numbered section '1 Abstract' — a second abstract running task by task ('For task 1, we build two models to measure the pulse and temperature of higher education system in different countries') — so it is excluded with the summary sheet. The heading 'Background' is glued to the tail of block 21 and 'estatement' / 'ssumptions' to the tails of 22 / 23, so the section boundaries sit one block earlier than the body they label; this is why the chapter opens at the block that carries the background prose, not at a heading block. Block 22 is one 233-word measured paragraph spanning pp. 3-4. Functions: 22 background (Rising participation, graduate earnings premium, pandemic pressure) with no quantity of its own; 23 restates the four tasks and the two-aspect reading of health; 34 argues strength is not health (Nobel-laureate example: past achievement, talent flows) which is why fitness-for-purpose indicators are dropped; 35 states the substantive definition (inclusive ability of the youth plus coordination with the national economy); 36 splits health into status quo of industry performance and improvement potential; 37-38 define the three status-quo dimensions (coverage, fairness, achievement) with 37 ending in a page footer; 39 Figure 3 caption (coverage cornerstone, fairness basis); 40 defines the three potential dimensions (input, output, efficiency) inside the same block that introduces them; 41 Figure 4 caption. Note the paper's own claim in 34 that health indicators must exclude 'past achievement' while Table 1 keeps two historical-growth indicators (grc over 30 years, dgr cohort completion).

heading: 2.3 Assumptions (ten numbered assumptions)
note: Ten assumptions, one measured block each, all asserting a boundary on what the models may claim, hence ten limits: (1) higher education irreplaceable by basic education, so coverage matters; (2) quantity is prerequisite for quality, per-capita quality gaps compensable by scale; (3) all sectors' investment measurable in currency; (4) unfairness comes from economic factors and social status; (5) buyer's labour market, degree premium drives demand; (6) policies exclude electoral promises and require legislative backing; (7) absent strong policy, indicators move slowly, which licenses the two-year window used for missing data; (8) public institutions pursue justice, private ones efficiency; (9) same indexes in different statistical calibers trend alike; (10) COVID-19 and financial shocks excluded. Assumption 8 is the one later invoked — but block 81 cites it as 'hypothesis 9', and 'hypothesis 9' in this list is the statistical-caliber assumption, so the paper is off by one wherever it renumbers. No assumption is justified by evidence; assumption 7 is the only one that changes the data pipeline (missing-value window of +-2 years). Block 33 carries the '2.3 Problem Analysis' heading in its tail.

heading: 3 Evaluation System & Model — 3.1 Construction of Evaluation System (3.1.1 System A, 3.1.2 System B; Tables 1-2)
note: Construction chapter, two indicator systems. Group 1 is [42,43] because block 42 is a watermark run and block 43 is the page footer 'Page 7' welded to the real headings '3 Evaluation System & Model' and '3.1 Construction of Evaluation System'. 44 states the two-model plan keyed to the two aspects; 45 is the 3.1.1 heading alone; 46-47 assign System A to the status quo and fix coverage/fairness/achievement as primary indicators; 48 enumerates System A's secondaries (three coverage, two fairness, four ability-distribution plus doctoral rate). 49 and 53 are Panel A/Panel B axis dumps of Figure 5 (literacy, numeracy proficiency of 16-34 year-olds); 50-51 are watermark plus 'Page 8' folded into group 8 with Panel B's title; 52 and 54 (caption, 'Proficiency distribution among graduates younger than 35 (2012 or 2015)') are figure reads. The figure lists Flanders* and Netherlands* with asterisks that are never explained, and Flanders is not one of the 21 countries, so the indicator's denominator population (21 OECD members) and the figure's population differ. Group 11 [55] is prose plus the glued header row of Table 1 ('Abbreviation of / First level / Secondary / Secondary indicators / Data processing / indicator / indicators'): it explains the Survey of Adult Skills five proficiency groups and the ad-a..ad-d processing rule. Group 12 is the table body, 20 rows, each row split into 2-5 measured blocks (pcy, rmu, grc, pfe, pou, ad-a..ad-d, dgr) because every cell wraps; group 13 is the caption, printed after the rows. Caption position after the table body is the same for Table 2. 77-80 start System B (improvement potential; input 3, output 6, efficiency) with block 80 spanning pp. 9-10 and ending in the page footer. 81 is the only argumentative block here: the public-expenditure share measures efficiency because private providers chase efficiency under 'hypothesis 9' (actually assumption 8). Table 2 body is 24 blocks for 11 indicator codes, and the codes collide: 'pef' labels both the input indicator (public higher-education expenditure as a share of total public expenditure) and the efficiency indicator (share of public expenditure on institutions), and 'PCT'/'ppa' sit in one row ('Proportion of PCT ... PCT ppa applications published'), so the abbreviation column does not identify 11 distinct variables even though footnote 2 claims 11 potential indicators. Table 1 has 10 codes as claimed.

heading: 3.2 Evaluation Model — 3.2.1 Task1 Analysis, 3.2.2 Statement of Model (IEW-TOPSIS), 3.2.3 Result of Serval nations
note: The model chapter is the worst-fragmented range in this paper: from block 109 to 170 almost every block is a single printed line of a prose bullet or a displayed formula, because the page is set in a two-column layout with inline math. Groups follow paragraph and step continuity, not the measured line count. 109-113 is one bullet whose marker '⚫' is its own zero-word block and whose sentence runs across five lines: factors chosen -> IEW-TOPSIS used to turn both systems into models. 114-115 is the second bullet (applied to all 21 countries, ranked, bar chart) and carries the 3.2.2 heading in its tail. 116 argues for IEW-TOPSIS and contains two factual errors: it dates Shannon's 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' to 1984 (it is 1948) and asserts the method 'is applicable to any country in the world' although TOPSIS scores are relative to the comparison set, which is why the 21-country frame matters. 117 introduces the seven IEW steps; 118-137 are step i (119 selects n countries and m indicators; 120-122 are footnote 1 — the list of the 21 countries, broken by a watermark and the 'Page 12' footer, continuing in 141 — plus the index range), steps ii-vi as derivation blocks with the normalisation formulas for positive and negative indicators, the proportion p_ij, entropy e_j with k=1/ln(n), redundancy d_j=1-e_j and weight w_j. 141 holds footnotes 1 (continued: Israel through United States, completing 21), 2 (10 status-quo and 11 potential indicators), 3 (only the student-teacher ratio is negative) and 4 (redundancy). Counting the two halves of footnote 1 gives exactly 21 countries, matching Figure 6's 21 axis labels, but Figure 6 marks Estonia*, Norway* (and Figure 5 also Netherlands*, Flanders*) with asterisks that are never explained. 142-144 is watermark plus 'Page 13' plus the continuation of the convergence sentence; 145 gives the high/low-quality conversion, 146-148 the vector normalisation Z_ij, 149 the Z matrix, 150-155 best/worst solutions Z+ and Z-, 156-161 the weighted distances D_i+ / D_i- and closeness C_i = D_i-/(D_i+ + D_i-). 162 is footnote 5 on high/low-quality indicators. 163-167 is watermark, 'Page 14' footer and the grade construction: four equal bands poor 0.000-0.249, fair 0.250-0.499, Good 0.500-0.749, excellent 0.750-1.000. 165 contains the typo 'The values of C table ate between 0 and 1'. 168 is step v (sort by C_i), 169-170 the Python solve and ranking with the 3.2.3 heading in 170's tail. 171 restates the model's scope, 172 reports the computed proximities, 173 interprets the distribution: 11 countries above 0.5 and 10 below, 'only 2 countries exceed 0.6', highest Slovak Republic 0.639816, lowest Israel 0.264504. That reading is internally consistent (11+10=21) but it means no country reaches the Good band — the whole sample is poor/fair — and the paper never remarks on it, although later (285) it treats an average-level target as 'achievable and reasonable'. 174 is the Table 3 caption; the table itself is a raster, so no score column could be checked against 173 and the per-country values are only available for Chile (208). 175 reports the second model run, 176 is the Figure 6 axis dump (21 labels). No notation table exists anywhere in the paper; every symbol is introduced inline inside these derivation blocks.

heading: 3.3 Sensitivity Analysis of Models (Figures 7-8)
note: Short chapter, one experiment. 177 is the Figure 6 caption carrying the 3.3 heading in its tail. 178 states that both models are perturbed. 179 defines the sensitivity criterion and the design in one block: Chile as subject, weights held fixed, each indicator raised individually, score response speed read as sensitivity — note this is a one-at-a-time design on a single country, so it cannot speak to weight sensitivity or to joint perturbations. 180 is the Figure 7 caption, 181-183 bundle a watermark and the 'Page 16' footer with the Figure 8 caption. 184 draws the conclusion: the score is not sensitive to any single indicator, so several indicators must move together, hence several policies; it also carries the '4 Application' heading in its tail. The inference is a non-result used as a design premise — no elasticity, threshold or numeric sensitivity value is reported anywhere, and neither figure is accompanied by a table of the perturbed amounts.

heading: 4 Application — 4.1 Statement of Application under Tasks, 4.2 Solution of Task 2 & 3
note: Two sub-sections of the application. 185 is the 4.1 heading; 186-207 are five bullets of the task roadmap, each bullet a zero-word '⚫' marker plus 3-8 measured lines, regrouped accordingly (186-193, 194-196, 197-200, 201-205, 206-207). The fourth bullet is the only one that reports an operation rather than announcing one: after the policy, four indicators are set to target, the model is re-run and compared with the pre-policy run to test effectiveness (hence compute). 207 ends with the '4.2 Solution of Task 2 & 3' heading and a stray marker. 208-213 reports Task 2: Chile scores 0.279497 on industry performance and 0.73439 on improvement potential, the largest gap of the 21 countries, which is taken as evidence for the inverse relationship; 213 ends in an unlabelled axis dump '0.8 0.7 ... 0'. 214 is the two-series legend and 215 the Figure 9 caption (both figure reads). 216 interprets the choice of Chile with three reasons (near-lowest performance, highest potential, clearest inverse relation). Task 3: 217-220 announce the indicator-by-indicator comparison against the all-country average and the radar chart; 221-222 are the chart title and legend, 223-224 the axis labels (pcy, rmu, grc, pfe, pou, ad-a..ad-d, dgr — exactly the ten System A indicators), 225 the Figure 10 caption. 226 reads the figure: only GRC exceeds the all-country average. 227 is the methodological check that carries the weight of the next block: comparing a country to a cross-country mean is only meaningful if the mean represents the group, so low dispersion (low coefficient of variation) is required. 228 then reports standard deviations and coefficients of variation and concludes that rmu, pfe, pou and dgr have small coefficients of variation, so their all-country means represent them, and it fixes those means as the vision target: rmu 0.36357355, pfe 0.54955861, 'pu' (sic, for pou) 71.21904762, dgr 1.857142857, against Chile's 0.114992569, 0.281632653, 15.4 and 0.3. The targets are therefore 1.9x to 6.2x Chile's current values — large jumps justified only by the claim, since no coefficient-of-variation number is printed. The four indicators are also exactly the ones found deficient in 226, so the small-CV filter and the policy set coincide rather than being independent selection steps. These targets are what produce the 0.444658 in 281-284.

heading: 4.3 Necessary of Policy with GM (GM(1,1) forecast, Figure 11)
note: Necessity argument before the policy list. 229 is the heading block; 230 fixes the demonstration series (ratio of master's to bachelor's students, rmu) and its purpose. 231 is the data-provenance block: the series comes from Chile's Ministry of Education database, the caliber differs from the OECD's, and the gap is waved through by 'our hypothesis' — which is assumption 9, the statistical-caliber assumption, so the argument leans on the same off-by-one citation seen at block 81. 232 names the window: 2007-2018 published, 2019-2028 forecast. 233-234 give three reasons for grey prediction (few points, grey causality, testability) as one group because they are a three-item list split by the measure. 235 reports that GM(1,1) was run after a passed level-ratio deviation test, in Python, with the code relegated to an appendix — no parameter values, no level-ratio statistics and no residuals are printed, so the forecast cannot be checked. 236-237 bundle the chart title 'The trend of B-S ratio under GM(1,1)' with a watermark; 238 is the Figure 11 caption. 239 interprets: from 2016 to 2028 the ratio rises only about 46% in 12 years, below the vision target, hence strong policy is imperative; it also carries the '4.4 Solution of Task 5' heading in its tail. Two defects sit in that sentence: the forecast window is 2019-2028 while the quoted change is 2016-2028 (12 years), mixing the observed and forecast periods, and 'was the youngest of data samples of 21 OECD countries' means the Chilean ratio starts from the lowest base, which makes any percentage growth look larger, not smaller.

heading: 4.4 Solution of Task 5 (policy recommendations i-iv, specific policies and timetable, Figure 12)
note: Policy chapter; each numbered recommendation is one group, reflowed from 4-6 measured lines. i) raise government investment in quality (conditions, resources, subsidies to poor students) over 240-245; ii) strengthen private-institution management and assessment standards, screening out inferior providers, 246-249 (246 spans pp. 19-20, breaking after 'Through strict'); iii) de-profit the education system, channelling resources to public institutions to rebuild equity after years of marketisation, 250-255; iv) relax graduate-enrolment growth limits so pandemic-hit graduates can be absorbed, cutting unemployment and stabilising demand, 256-258. All four are handed forward to the government, not solved in the model, so all four are handoffs. 259 is the transition sentence to the timetable. 260-263 are the concrete measure paragraphs: 260 defers epidemic control and economic revival as beyond the paper's argument (an explicit scope handoff), 261 states the assessment/rating architecture (institution evaluation, professional certification), 262 tax relief plus buying bonds of highly rated institutions to close funding gaps, 263 addresses the polarised distribution of educational resources through a three-party arrangement (government funding, institutions teaching, enterprises hiring). No cost, instrument size or legal vehicle is attached to any measure, and none is mapped back to the four indicators that the vision targets. 264 is the Figure 12 caption; the timetable itself is an image and its schedule is not in the text layer, so the promised timing could not be checked against the GM horizon (2019-2028) or against the 12-year claim in 239.

heading: 4.5 Solution of Task 4 & 6 (policy effectiveness re-evaluation)
note: Effectiveness test. 265 is the 4.5 heading. 266-271 restates the vision (raise the four affected indicators to the all-country average) and the policy bundle already proposed; 272-280 is the experiment as executed: replace rmu, pfe, pou and dgr for Chile with the target values, feed the adjusted matrix into the Task 1 IEW-TOPSIS model, re-run in Python, extract Chile's closeness and compare with the original run. 281-284 reports the result: 0.279497 -> 0.444658, described as a significant improvement. The number is arithmetically checkable only against the target construction, and it is worth stating what it means in the paper's own grade bands: 0.444658 stays inside 'fair' (0.250-0.499), so the modelled country remains below the Good threshold even after every targeted indicator is lifted to the sample average — consistent with 173's finding that no country in the sample is above 0.6. 285-291 is the paper's defence: the score is not high because the target was set at the average rather than the best, and an achievable target is preferred; a significant increase is taken as sufficient evidence of effectiveness. The block also promises that 'Gray Model of the time variables will be presented in the next part of Model II', but the next section is Task 7 (stakeholder impacts) and no time-variable GM model appears anywhere after it, so this handoff is never delivered. 291 ends in watermark, page footer and the '4.6 Solution of Task 7' heading.

heading: 4.6 Solution of Task 7 (impacts on students, faculties, schools, community, country)
note: Five stakeholder sections, one group each, each group's blocks being consecutive printed lines of a single paragraph: i) students 292-297 (better teaching, loans and subsidies widening access, de-profitisation lowering private costs); ii) faculties 298-303 (entry assessment raising staff quality, tenure evaluation against laziness, de-profitisation lifting pay instead of squeezing it); iii) schools 304-308 (resources attract talent, higher human capital in the teaching body); iv) community 309-317 (equity reduces rich-poor and regional gaps, human-capital spillovers, more high-quality local institutions); v) country 318-329 plus continuation 333-337 after the page break — soft power, the fairness damage of marketisation, absorbing unemployed graduates into postgraduate study, human capital, ageing, international student flows and cultural diplomacy. Every group is mechanism-talk: each names a policy and the causal channel by which it acts, none carries a magnitude, and none is linked back to an indicator in either system, so the Task 7 answer is a qualitative counterpart to the quantitative Tasks 1-6. 330 is footnote 6, a definition of human capital (education, health, domestic mobility, immigration expenditure) attached to the human-capital mention in 307, so it is a define inside a results run. Group 7 is [331,332,333,334,335,336,337] because a watermark and the 'Page 23' footer split the country paragraph mid-sentence ('...the young people will have a / higher level of knowledge...'); 337 carries the '5 Verification' heading in its tail.

heading: 5 Verification (inverse-relationship test, Figure 13)
note: The verification chapter is one logical test, stated as a falsifiable criterion and then inspected on a scatter. 338 is the '5 Verification' heading block. 339 is the criterion: if performance status and improvement potential are inversely related, the evaluation model reflects health as the two definitions imply — so the test is internal consistency between the model's own two outputs, not agreement with any external measure, and the paper is explicit that this is what 'verification' means here. 340 reports the Stata run producing the figure; 341 is the Figure 13 caption. 342-343 interprets the roughly inverse correlation with the substantive reason (present performance versus future room), 342 spanning pp. 23-24. 344 is the exception block: countries in the lower-left and upper-right regions are 'double high or double low', contradicting the inverse reading, and the proposed remedy is to fit an approximate functional relation to identify such countries — i.e. the counterexamples are acknowledged and deferred, not resolved. The chapter therefore establishes that the two scores usually move opposite, which is close to a construction property of the two indicator systems (status quo measured with level indicators, potential measured with input-output-efficiency gaps), and it does not test the model against any external assessment of higher-education health.

heading: 5.1 Strengths, 5.2 Disadvantages; references and data links follow the last block
note: Self-assessment chapter. 345 announces the strength list and holds item i's marker; the five strengths are 345-350 (IEW is objective, immune to Delphi/AHP bias), 351-355 (TOPSIS needs no objective function, no distributional assumption, handles small samples and many units), 356-359 (IEW-TOPSIS improves on plain TOPSIS and separates the two aspects), 360 (GM needs little data) and 361-362 (system and model distinguish status quo from coordination, item v). The '5.2 Disadvantages' heading is glued to the tail of 362; 363 announces the weakness list and holds item i. Weaknesses: 363-366 (IEW cannot reduce dimensionality; entropy method degenerates when values barely move or jump), 367-369 (TOPSIS indicator selection is hard, needs the right number of uncertain indicators and more than two objects; GM series not smooth, larger forecast error), 370-373 (system and model do not reflect input-output coordination; only some indicators selected; policy effects take long and pass through other factors). Item v is the honest one and it undercuts the paper's central claim: the two 'systems' are presented as complementary halves of health, yet the model never models the coordination between them, which is exactly what the problem statement asked for. 373 carries the 'Reference' heading in its tail. Not coded as chapters: references [1]-[6] (blocks 374-379) and the three data links (380), which follow the body without discussion.
